title: Leadership team effectiveness: what the research says
description: What makes a leadership team effective: the conditions, ways of working and team states research points to, and how to judge the result.
h1: What makes a leadership team effective?
lead: Effective leadership teams get the conditions right first, then how they work; trust and psychological safety grow out of both. The conditions are a real team with a clear purpose, tasks that need the whole team, the right size and members, and support. How they work means prepared meetings with clear goals, focused dialogue, conflict about tasks rather than people, acting as one team, and learning. Judge the result by direction, alignment and commitment, by whether the team can keep working well together, and by whether its members grow.
takeaways: Get the conditions right first: a real team, a clear purpose, work that needs everyone, the right members, and support.
Then work on the meetings. Clear goals for each item and focused discussion go with better results in top teams.
Psychological safety, trust and cohesion matter, and they build up from how the team is set up and how it works.
Judge effectiveness by direction, alignment and commitment, by the team's ability to keep working together, and by members' growth.
Many senior groups are not real teams. Decide which issues truly need the whole team, and handle the rest elsewhere.

blocks.text: What is leadership team effectiveness?

Leadership team effectiveness is how well a leadership team does the work only it can do, while staying able to do it again. Research on teams spans more than fifty years and thousands of studies (Kozlowski and Ilgen, 2006). Reviews of it now describe a chain: inputs, then the processes and states that carry their effect, then outcomes (Mathieu et al., 2008).

It helps to read a leadership team in four layers. Conditions are how the team is set up. Processes are how it works, mostly in meetings. States are what builds up between members over time. Outcomes are what the team produces and what it leaves behind.

items.title: Conditions
items.text: How the team is set up: membership, purpose, tasks, size and support.

items.title: Processes
items.text: How it works, mostly in meetings: goals, focus, dialogue and decisions.

items.title: States
items.text: What builds up between members over time: safety, trust and cohesion.

blocks.text: How do you judge whether a leadership team is effective?

Hackman proposed three tests for any team (Haas and Mortensen, 2016). First, does its output satisfy the people who receive it? Second, does the way it works keep it able to work well together? Third, do its members learn and develop through being part of it?

blocks.text: For a leadership team, the people who receive its work are the rest of the organisation. Drath and colleagues argue that leadership shows itself in three outcomes for a group: direction, alignment and commitment (Drath et al., 2008). Direction is shared agreement on what the group is trying to achieve. Alignment is work that is coordinated. Commitment is members' willingness to make the success of the whole a priority, not only their own success.

Put together, these give a leadership team three questions to ask itself. Does the organisation get clear direction, aligned work and commitment from us? Are we still able to work well together? Are we, as individuals, getting better at leading?

blocks.title: A question for your team
blocks.text: If each of the people who report to us described our direction in one sentence, how many different sentences would we hear?
Why is a leadership team harder to make effective than other teams?

Katzenbach argued that even in well-run companies, the group at the top seldom works as a real team (Katzenbach, 1997). He gave several reasons. A meaningful collective purpose is hard to define at the top, and goals tend to be broad. Members are often chosen for their position rather than for the skills a shared task needs.

Executives are also used to being accountable for their own units, and mutual accountability can feel foreign. A group run by a single leader is often faster, and it fits the hierarchy. Katzenbach did not conclude that top teams are pointless. His advice was to tell team work from other work, and to handle each in its own way.

Later research points the same way. Wageman, Nunes, Burruss and Hackman studied more than 100 senior teams around the world (Wageman et al., 2008). They describe executives who put their own functions ahead of the team's shared work. In an interview about that research, Hackman said that almost every team believed its membership was clear. Yet when the researchers asked members to describe the team, fewer than 10 per cent agreed on its membership (Coutu, 2009).
Both accounts point to a double role. Each member leads a unit and is judged on it. The leadership team asks them to put the whole organisation first, usually for a few hours a week.
What conditions does an effective leadership team need?

Hackman's work on teams names five conditions (Hackman, 2002). They are a real team, a compelling direction, an enabling structure, a supportive organisation and expert coaching. For senior teams, Wageman and colleagues treat three as essential: a real team, a compelling purpose and the right people. Structure, support and coaching then help the team make the most of them (Wageman et al., 2008).

items: **A real team.** Members know who is on the team and who is not. Hackman warned that a very large senior team may be worse than no team at all (Coutu, 2009). His example was one holding all the chief executive's direct reports.

**A clear purpose.** The team needs a purpose of its own, not the sum of its members' jobs. Start from [the purpose of a leadership team](/articles/leadership-team-purpose) and the issues that need everyone.
**Tasks that need the whole team.** Katzenbach's test is a collective work product: a result that draws on members' different skills, which none could produce alone (Katzenbach, 1997).

**The right size and members.** Members should bring the skills the shared work needs, not only a senior title. Hackman's rule of thumb was no double digits (Coutu, 2009); see [leadership team size](/articles/how-big-should-a-leadership-team-be).

**Information and support.** The team needs data, time and help for its shared work, and coaching aimed at the team as a whole. Hackman reported that coaching individual executives did little to help senior teams perform better (Coutu, 2009).

blocks.title: A rule of thumb
blocks.text: If an agenda item could be settled by one member and the chief executive, it does not need the whole team. Keep the team's time for the issues only the team can solve.
How does an effective leadership team work together?

Most of a leadership team's shared work happens in meetings, so that is where its processes show. One study combined members' ratings with observers' data from eight top management groups and 56 agenda items (Bang et al., 2010). Goal clarity and focused communication were both linked to higher team effectiveness.

The same study found that speaking up when an item's goal was unclear helped. It went with more focused communication, better task performance and better relationships. Calling out a discussion that had drifted off track did not help performance, and it went with poorer relationships.

A broader study videotaped 92 regular team meetings (Kauffeld and Lehmann-Willenbrock, 2012). Teams with more problem-solving talk and action planning were more satisfied with their meetings, and better meetings went with higher team productivity. Criticising and complaining showed negative links that were stronger than the positive ones. For a practical format, see [leadership team meeting agenda](/articles/leadership-team-meeting-agenda).

blocks.text: Meetings also need room for people to speak. Bang interviewed 21 executives from seven top teams about why they stayed silent when a meeting lost its way (Bang, 2012). Their silence rested mainly on a belief that speaking up would be seen as negative and bring unwelcome consequences.
Disagree about the work, not about each other

A meta-analysis of 116 studies found that relationship conflict was consistently linked to poorer group outcomes (de Wit et al., 2012). Task conflict was not strongly negative overall, and its link with performance was more positive in top management teams. The detail is in [task conflict and relationship conflict](/articles/task-conflict-and-relationship-conflict).
Act as one team, and keep learning

Researchers call the first of these behavioural integration: how far a top team engages in mutual and collective interaction. A study of 402 firms found that the chief executive, the team and the firm each played a part (Simsek et al., 2005).

Learning is the other habit. In a study of 51 work teams, learning behaviour carried the link between psychological safety and team performance (Edmondson, 1999). Support from the organisation and coaching by the team leader also shaped outcomes.
What role do psychological safety, trust and cohesion play?

These are states, not actions. Shared properties of a team emerge from how members interact, and from selection, socialisation and leadership (Kozlowski and Klein, 2000). A team cannot simply decide to have them. It can shape the conditions and meetings they grow from.

Psychological safety is a shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking (Edmondson, 1999). In Edmondson's study it went with more learning behaviour, which in turn went with better performance. See [psychological safety in leadership teams](/articles/psychological-safety-in-leadership-teams).

Trust has a solid record too. Across 112 studies of 7,763 teams, trust among members was positively related to team performance (De Jong et al., 2016). This held even after allowing for past performance. The strength of the link depended on factors such as how interdependent the team's tasks were. More is in [how to build trust in a leadership team](/articles/how-to-build-trust-in-a-leadership-team).

Cohesion matters as well, with a twist. Across studies, it related more strongly to performance measured as behaviour than as outcomes (Beal et al., 2003). The link was also stronger where work flowed intensively between members. For a leadership team whose members mostly work apart, that is worth noting.
How do you build a high-performing leadership team?
Work through the layers in order. The steps below turn the research into practice; adapt them to your team.

items.title: Decide where you need a team
items.text: List the decisions and work that need everyone, and send the rest to individuals or smaller groups.

items.title: Settle who is on it
items.text: Name the members, and check that every member would give the same list.

items.title: Agree the purpose together
items.text: A [leadership team charter](/articles/leadership-team-charter) is one way to record purpose, members and ways of working.

items.title: Give every meeting item a stated goal
items.text: Say whether it is for information, discussion or decision, and keep the discussion on that goal.

items.title: Make disagreement about the work normal
items.text: Ask for the strongest case against a proposal before you decide.

items.title: Review how you work
items.text: Spend ten minutes at the end of a meeting on what helped and what got in the way.

items.title: Measure, then talk
items.text: A short anonymous survey of every member gives a starting point; see [how to assess a leadership team](/articles/how-to-assess-a-leadership-team).

blocks.text: What can you do this month?
Pick one layer and test it in your next two meetings. Each of these takes minutes, and each tells you something.

items: Ask each member, privately, to list who is on the leadership team. Compare the lists.
Ask which three issues this quarter need all of you, and which issues do not.
Give every agenda item a one-line goal and an owner, and check at the end whether you met it.
Close one meeting by asking what each member held back, and what would have made it easier to say.

blocks.title: A question for your team
blocks.text: What do we do together that none of us could do alone, and how much of our meeting time goes on it?
